pt-economy.title: pt-economy.c0.text
Portugal's economy: Portugal's economy produces about €285 billion of goods and services a year, under 2% of the EU total. Services such as tourism, trade and finance dominate.\n\nExports now equal close to half of GDP, far more than in the past, so the country depends heavily on selling abroad.

pt-economy.title: pt-economy.c1.title
Portugal's economy: From EU entry to the euro

pt-economy.title: pt-economy.c1.text
Portugal's economy: Joining the European Community in 1986 opened markets and brought large EU funds, and Portugal grew fast for about 15 years.\n\nAfter the euro arrived in 1999, growth slowed sharply. The 2000s became a "lost decade" in which the economy barely grew while debts piled up.

pt-economy.title: pt-economy.c2.text
Portugal's economy: In 2011, unable to borrow on the markets at affordable rates, Portugal asked the EU and the IMF for a rescue loan. Three years of spending cuts, tax rises and reforms followed.\n\nThe economy has since recovered: unemployment fell, the state ran budget surpluses in several years and public debt dropped below 100% of GDP.

pt-economy.title: pt-economy.c3.text
Portugal's economy: Tourism is one of Portugal's biggest industries. Visitors come for beaches, cities, food, golf and history, and in 2024 tourist lodgings recorded about 31 million guests.\n\nSpending by foreign visitors, about €27 billion a year, makes tourism the country's largest single export.

pt-economy.title: pt-economy.c4.text
Portugal's economy: Portugal's goods exports are more varied than many people think. Cars and components lead, followed by machinery, refined fuels, plastics, paper, textiles and shoes.\n\nMost go to other EU countries, above all Spain, as Portuguese firms plug into European supply chains.

pt-economy.title: pt-economy.c5.text
Portugal's economy: Portugal is the world's largest producer and exporter of cork, selling about €1.2 billion of it abroad each year.\n\nMost becomes wine stoppers, but cork also goes into floors, insulation, shoes and even spacecraft. Nothing is wasted: offcuts are ground into granules and pressed into new products.

pt-economy.title: pt-economy.c6.text
Portugal's economy: Portugal makes around 7 million hectolitres of wine a year, among the world's top dozen producers, and exports close to €1 billion of it.\n\nPort is still the best-known product, but table wines now earn more abroad in total. The industry's aim is to sell fewer cheap bulk wines and more bottles at higher prices.

pt-economy.title: pt-economy.c7.text
Portugal's economy: Portugal is one of Europe's leaders in clean electricity. In 2024 renewables, mainly hydro, wind and solar, supplied around 70% of the electricity the country used.\n\nIts last coal power station closed in 2021, and governments have set targets to go higher still by 2030.

pt-economy.title: pt-economy.c8.text
Portugal's economy: Since the mid-2010s, Lisbon and Porto have become popular bases for tech start-ups and remote workers.\n\nThe Web Summit, one of the world's largest tech conferences, has been held in Lisbon every November since 2016. A handful of companies with Portuguese founders have grown into "unicorns" valued at over $1 billion.

pt-economy.title: pt-economy.c9.text
Portugal's economy: Wages in Portugal are among the lower ones in Western Europe. The national minimum wage has risen quickly, to €920 a month in 2026, paid 14 times a year.\n\nThe deeper issue is productivity: each hour worked produces much less value than the EU average, which limits how far pay can rise.

pt-economy.title: pt-food.c0.text
Portugal's economy: Portugal and Galicia share what nutritionists call the Atlantic diet: plenty of fish, vegetables, potatoes, bread and olive oil, with a little wine, eaten slowly with family.\n\nIt looks like the Mediterranean diet, but it leans more on the sea, on cabbage and potatoes, and on soups and stews cooked for hours.

pt-economy.title: pt-food.c0.viz.items.3
Portugal's economy: Slow stews shared at the table

pt-economy.title: pt-food.c1.text
Portugal's economy: Portugal's favourite fish doesn't live in Portuguese waters. Fishermen sailed to Newfoundland and Greenland to catch cod, salting it on board so it would keep for months.\n\nToday most bacalhau comes from Norway and Iceland, but the Portuguese way of salting, drying and soaking it remains a national ritual.

pt-economy.title: pt-food.c2.text
Portugal's economy: Grilled sardines are the smell of a Portuguese summer. They are best from about June to October, when they are fat and oily, and are eaten on a slice of bread that soaks up the juices.\n\nPortugal is also famous for tinned fish: canneries have packed sardines, tuna and mackerel in olive oil since the 19th century.

pt-economy.title: pt-food.c3.text
Portugal's economy: Portugal is small, but each region cooks differently. The green, rainy north eats hearty soups, tripe and cured meats; the centre roasts suckling pig; the Alentejo makes bread soups and pork dishes; the Algarve cooks fish and shellfish.\n\nThe islands add their own: stews cooked in volcanic ground in the Azores, and beef skewers on bay-wood sticks in Madeira.

pt-economy.title: pt-food.c4.text
Portugal's economy: Olive oil, azeite, is the fat of Portuguese cooking. It dresses fish and boiled potatoes, finishes soups and is poured generously over bacalhau.\n\nPortugal has become one of the world's leading producers, mainly thanks to new irrigated groves in the Alentejo. Traditional varieties such as Galega and Cobrançosa give oils from mild to peppery.

pt-economy.title: pt-food.c5.text
Portugal's economy: Portugal's best-known cheeses are made from ewe's milk and set not with animal rennet but with the flowers of a wild thistle. The result is often soft, creamy and slightly bitter.\n\nSerra da Estrela is the most famous, but Azeitão, Nisa, Évora and São Jorge from the Azores all have protected status.

pt-economy.title: pt-food.c6.text
Portugal's economy: Many Portuguese sweets were born in convents and monasteries. Nuns and monks used egg whites to starch linen and clear wine, leaving mountains of yolks, which they mixed with sugar from Madeira and Brazil.\n\nThe results have heavenly names: toucinho do céu, papos de anjo, barriga de freira. The pastel de nata is the most famous heir of this tradition.

pt-economy.title: pt-food.c7.text
Portugal's economy: Portugal packs very different wines into a small country. In the rainy Minho, Vinho Verde is light and fresh. Up the Douro valley, terraced schist slopes give port and powerful reds. On the hot Alentejo plains, wines are ripe and smooth.\n\nMost are made from native grapes found almost nowhere else, such as Alvarinho, Touriga Nacional and Antão Vaz.

pt-economy.title: pt-food.c8.text
Portugal's economy: In Portugal, um café means a short, strong espresso, drunk standing at the counter in a minute or two, often several times a day. In Lisbon it's a bica, in Porto a cimbalino.\n\nCafés and pastelarias are neighbourhood living rooms. Coffee is cheap, usually about €1 or less, and roasted in a dark, smooth style shaped by Portugal's links with Brazil and Africa.

pt-economy.title: pt-food.c9.text
Portugal's economy: Japanese tempura probably owes its start to Portuguese traders and missionaries, who reached Japan in the 1540s. They fried fish and vegetables in batter, much like Portugal's peixinhos da horta, battered green beans.\n\nThe name may come from têmporas, the Ember Days, when Catholics avoided meat. Portuguese cooking also left its mark in Goa, Macau, Malacca and Brazil.

Portugal's economy: Fado, cante, the song of 25 April and folk instruments.

pt-economy.title: pt-fado.c0.text
Portugal's economy: Fado is Lisbon's urban song: a single voice, with the Portuguese guitar and a classical guitar, singing of love, jealousy, poverty, the sea and fate. The word comes from the Latin fatum, destiny.\n\nIt grew in the city's poor riverside districts in the 19th century, and UNESCO added it to its list of intangible heritage in 2011.

pt-economy.title: pt-fado.c0.viz.items.0
Portugal's economy: One voice, often in a black shawl

pt-economy.title: pt-fado.c0.viz.items.2
Portugal's economy: Songs of fate, love and loss

pt-economy.title: pt-fado.c1.text
Portugal's economy: The classic place to hear fado is a casa de fado, a small restaurant where singers take turns between courses. When the lights dim, waiters stop serving and the room falls silent.\n\nIn fado vadio, "vagrant fado", amateurs stand up to sing in neighbourhood taverns, keeping the tradition alive away from the tourist trail.

pt-economy.title: pt-fado.c2.text
Portugal's economy: Fado has two homes. In Lisbon, singers often set new poems to a stock of traditional melodies, such as the fado menor or fado corrido, and phrase them freely.\n\nCoimbra's fado grew in its university: composed songs sung by men at night, tied to student life, farewells and the city itself.

pt-economy.title: pt-fado.c3.text
Portugal's economy: In fado, "guitarra" means the pear-shaped Portuguese guitar, while "viola" is the ordinary six-string guitar. The guitarra answers the singer's lines; the viola keeps the harmony and pulse.\n\nThe players follow the singer closely, since melodies stretch and pause. Instrumental pieces called guitarradas let the guitarra shine on its own.

pt-economy.title: pt-fado.c4.text
Portugal's economy: Amália Rodrigues (1920–1999) took fado from Lisbon's taverns to concert halls across the world. Born into a poor family, she sold fruit on the Lisbon docks as a girl before her voice made her a star.\n\nShe sang great poets, worked with composers who widened fado's sound, and remains the voice most people link with Portugal.

pt-economy.title: pt-fado.c5.text
Portugal's economy: Under the dictatorship, fado lyrics had to be approved by censors before being sung in public, and professional singers needed an official licence. Fado moved from the streets into licensed fado houses.\n\nThe regime favoured a tidy, patriotic fado, and after 1974 some saw it as the old regime's music. It took years for fado to lose that label.

pt-economy.title: pt-fado.c6.text
Portugal's economy: Cante alentejano, the unaccompanied group singing of the Alentejo, joined UNESCO's list in 2014. Its songs, called modas, are slow and spacious, like the plains they come from.\n\nOnce sung in fields, mines and taverns, cante now lives in choirs, festivals and schools, and young groups mix it with new music.

pt-economy.title: pt-fado.c7.text
Portugal's economy: Just after midnight on 25 April 1974, Rádio Renascença played José Afonso's "Grândola, Vila Morena". It was the second signal for army officers to begin the coup that ended 48 years of dictatorship.\n\nThe song, about brotherhood and equality in an Alentejo town, became the anthem of the Carnation Revolution and is still sung at every 25 April celebration.

pt-economy.title: pt-fado.c8.text
Portugal's economy: Beyond fado, Portuguese folk music uses a family of local instruments: the small cavaquinho, regional guitars called violas, bagpipes in the north-east and square drums in the Beira.\n\nEach region has its own sound. Many of these instruments nearly vanished in the 20th century and have been revived by folk groups and young musicians.

pt-economy.title: pt-fado.c9.text
Portugal's economy: Portuguese music today mixes old and new. Since the late 1990s, a generation of fadistas has brought fado back to young audiences, often with new instruments and poets.\n\nLisbon is also a hub for sounds from Angola, Cape Verde and Brazil, while pop, rap and folk artists sing in Portuguese with growing confidence.

pt-economy.title: pt-fado.c9.viz.items.0
Portugal's economy: New fado: young voices, new poets

pt-economy.title: pt-architecture.c0.text
Portugal's economy: Portugal's oldest great churches are Romanesque, built mostly in the 12th and 13th centuries as the kingdom took shape. They have thick granite walls, round arches and small windows.\n\nCathedrals such as those of Lisbon, Porto and Coimbra look like castles, with battlements, because they were built in a time of war.

pt-economy.title: pt-architecture.c1.text
Portugal's economy: King Afonso Henriques gave Alcobaça to Cistercian monks in 1153. Its church, begun in 1178, was one of the first Gothic buildings in Portugal.\n\nIts long, bare, white nave reflects Cistercian ideals of simplicity. Inside lie the carved tombs of King Pedro I and Inês de Castro, Portugal's most famous lovers.

pt-economy.title: pt-architecture.c2.text
Portugal's economy: King João I promised a monastery to the Virgin Mary if he won the Battle of Aljubarrota in 1385. The result, Batalha ("battle"), took over a century to build and is a masterpiece of Portuguese Gothic.\n\nIts chapter house has a vault about 19 metres wide with no central column, and its Unfinished Chapels are open to the sky.

pt-economy.title: pt-architecture.c3.text
Portugal's economy: Manueline is Portugal's own late Gothic style, from about 1490 to 1530, the age of King Manuel I. It covers doors, windows and columns with carved ropes, anchors, shells and coral.\n\nIt was paid for by the wealth of the sea route to India, and its decoration celebrates the voyages and the king's power.

pt-economy.title: pt-architecture.c3.viz.items.2
Portugal's economy: Cross of the Order of Christ

pt-economy.title: pt-architecture.c4.text
Portugal's economy: On the riverbank at Belém stand Portugal's two most famous Manueline buildings. The Jerónimos Monastery, begun in 1501, holds the tombs of Vasco da Gama and Luís de Camões.\n\nThe Belém Tower, built about 1514–1519, guarded the entrance to Lisbon's harbour. Both have been World Heritage Sites since 1983.

pt-economy.title: pt-architecture.c5.text
Portugal's economy: Azulejos moved from church interiors onto the outside of houses in the 19th century. Emigrants returning from Brazil, where tiled façades were common, are thought to have brought the fashion home, and factories made patterned tiles cheaply.\n\nTiles protect walls from rain and reflect light. Today whole streets in Lisbon, Porto, Aveiro and Ovar are wrapped in them.

pt-economy.title: pt-architecture.c6.text
Portugal's economy: After the 1755 earthquake, Lisbon's Baixa was rebuilt with the gaiola pombalina, a timber cage hidden inside masonry walls. Its diagonal braces help a building sway rather than burst apart.\n\nThe same planning ideas created a whole new town, Vila Real de Santo António in the Algarve, laid out from 1774.

pt-economy.title: pt-architecture.c7.text
Portugal's economy: The Estado Novo dictatorship (1933–1974) used architecture to project order and national pride. After an early modernist phase, it favoured a "Português Suave" style that dressed modern structures in traditional roofs, arches and stone.\n\nIts legacy includes courthouses, schools, housing estates, the Padrão dos Descobrimentos and the bridge over the Tagus, now called 25 de Abril.

pt-economy.title: pt-architecture.c8.text
Portugal's economy: Álvaro Siza (born 1933) and Eduardo Souto de Moura (born 1952) both won the Pritzker Prize, in 1992 and 2011. Both came from the "Porto School", shaped by Fernando Távora.\n\nTheir buildings are calm, precise and shaped by their sites: pools set among sea rocks, a stadium cut into a quarry, white walls that frame the light.

pt-economy.title: pt-architecture.c9.text
Portugal's economy: Portuguese pavement is still laid by hand, stone by stone, by craftsmen called calceteiros. White limestone and black basalt are cut into small cubes and set in sand to make waves, stars and ships.\n\nIn 2021 the craft was added to Portugal's national inventory of intangible heritage. But it is slippery when wet, and cities debate where to keep it.

pt-economy.title: pt-science.summary
Portugal's economy: From navigators' instruments to modern labs: Portugal's scientists and what they discovered.

pt-economy.title: pt-science.c0.text
Portugal's economy: Out of sight of land, 15th-century Portuguese pilots needed to know how far north or south they were. They found latitude by measuring the height of the Pole Star or the noon Sun.\n\nSimple instruments, printed rules and astronomical tables turned this into a routine that ordinary pilots could learn.

pt-economy.title: pt-science.c1.text
Portugal's economy: In 1542 the mathematician Pedro Nunes proposed a clever way to read angles more finely than the marks on an instrument allowed.\n\nHis idea, the nonius, used many concentric scales. Simplified a century later, it lives on in the vernier scale of every calliper.

pt-economy.title: pt-science.c2.text
Portugal's economy: Garcia de Orta was a Portuguese physician who lived in Goa for over 30 years. In 1563 he published the Colóquios, a book on the medicinal plants and drugs of Asia.\n\nWritten as lively dialogues, it tested old claims against what he saw, tasted and learnt from local healers.

pt-economy.title: pt-science.c3.text
Portugal's economy: In August 1709 Bartolomeu de Gusmão, a priest born in Brazil, showed King João V a small paper balloon lifted by hot air, indoors in Lisbon.\n\nHe also designed a bird-shaped airship, the Passarola. It almost certainly never flew, but it made him famous as "the Flying Priest".

pt-economy.title: pt-science.c4.text
Portugal's economy: Egas Moniz, neurologist and politician, won Portugal's first Nobel Prize in 1949 for the leucotomy, a brain operation for severe mental illness.\n\nThe operation was later abandoned, and his prize is still debated. His story is now used to teach how medicine should test new treatments.

pt-economy.title: pt-science.c5.text
Portugal's economy: Abel Salazar (1889–1946) was a Porto doctor and researcher who studied tissues under the microscope and invented a staining method.\n\nHe was also a painter and writer. In 1935 the dictatorship removed him from his university post for his ideas. He was no relation of the dictator Salazar.

pt-economy.title: pt-science.c6.text
Portugal's economy: Under the dictatorship, few Portuguese did research. After democracy returned in 1974, and especially from the 1990s, Portugal invested heavily in science.\n\nSpending on research more than tripled as a share of the economy, and thousands of young people were funded to earn doctorates at home and abroad.

pt-economy.title: pt-science.c7.text
Portugal's economy: Ciência Viva, created in 1996, is Portugal's agency for spreading scientific culture. It runs a network of about 20 science centres, from Bragança to the Algarve and the islands.\n\nIts flagship is the Pavilhão do Conhecimento in Lisbon, a hands-on science museum in a building from Expo '98.

pt-economy.title: pt-science.c8.text
Portugal's economy: When industrialist António Champalimaud died in 2004, he left about a quarter of his fortune, around €500 million, to create a foundation for medical research.\n\nIts Champalimaud Centre for the Unknown, opened in 2010 on the Tagus at Belém, studies the brain and cancer and treats patients.

pt-economy.title: pt-science.c9.text
Portugal's economy: Portuguese scientists today work in fields from neuroscience and cancer to ocean science, materials and space. Many institutes host international teams.\n\nPortugal is a member of CERN, the European Space Agency and the European Southern Observatory, and its researchers win competitive European grants.

pt-economy.title: pt-traditions.c0.text
Portugal's economy: Before Lent comes Carnaval, or Entrudo. Towns hold parades, children dress up, and Shrove Tuesday is often a day off, though not an official holiday.\n\nOld rural customs survive alongside Brazilian-style samba. In Podence, in Trás-os-Montes, masked caretos in bright woollen fringes run through the village shaking cowbells.

pt-economy.title: pt-traditions.c1.text
Portugal's economy: Easter is a major family feast in Portugal, especially in the north. In Braga, Holy Week brings solemn night processions that draw thousands of visitors.\n\nOn Easter Sunday, many villages receive the compasso, a small procession that visits homes with a cross. Godparents give their godchildren folar, a sweet or savoury Easter bread.

pt-economy.title: pt-traditions.c1.viz.items.0
Portugal's economy: Lent: fish, not meat, on Fridays

pt-economy.title: pt-traditions.c2.text
Portugal's economy: Lisbon's favourite saint is Santo António. On the night of 12 June every old neighbourhood becomes an arraial, a street party with grilled sardines, bifanas, beer and music.\n\nThe saint is known as a matchmaker and a finder of lost things, and each year the city hosts weddings in his name.

pt-economy.title: pt-traditions.c3.text
Portugal's economy: São João is Porto's biggest night. On 23 June the city stays out until dawn, tapping strangers on the head with plastic hammers, waving leeks, grilling sardines and eating caldo verde.\n\nAt midnight, fireworks burst over the Douro. Many people then walk to the sea at Foz to wait for sunrise. Braga also holds a huge São João.

pt-economy.title: pt-traditions.c4.text
Portugal's economy: São Pedro, on 29 June, closes the month of the popular saints. As Saint Peter was a fisherman, his feast is strongest in coastal towns.\n\nIn Póvoa de Varzim, neighbourhoods compete with decorated streets, cascatas and rusgas, groups of singers and dancers in fishermen's dress. Sintra, Montijo and Évora also hold big São Pedro fairs.

pt-economy.title: pt-traditions.c5.text
Portugal's economy: A romaria is a festival built around a pilgrimage to a chapel or shrine. It mixes a religious procession with a fair: brass bands, drums, folk dancing, stalls of sweets and fireworks.\n\nSummer is romaria season, above all in the north. Viana do Castelo's Senhora d'Agonia in August is one of the biggest, with streets carpeted in coloured sawdust and flowers.

pt-economy.title: pt-traditions.c6.text
Portugal's economy: On 1 November, All Saints' Day, children in many places go door to door asking for "pão por Deus", bread for God's sake, and receive bread, nuts, apples and sweets.\n\nOn 11 November, São Martinho, families gather for a magusto: chestnuts roasted over a fire, with young wine. A spell of mild weather around then is called the "summer of São Martinho".

pt-economy.title: pt-traditions.c7.text
Portugal's economy: Portugal's main Christmas meal is the consoada, on the night of 24 December. The classic menu is boiled bacalhau with cabbage, potatoes and eggs, all drizzled with olive oil and garlic.\n\nThen come sweets like rabanadas, sonhos and filhoses, and many families open presents at midnight. Bolo-rei, a ring-shaped fruit cake, stays on the table until 6 January.

pt-economy.title: pt-traditions.c8.text
Portugal's economy: The colourful clay rooster is Portugal's best-known souvenir, but it comes from a real craft tradition. Barcelos, in the Minho, has made pottery for centuries from the clay of the Cávado valley.\n\nBesides roosters, its potters model whole worlds in clay, called figurado: musicians, devils, animals and village scenes, often full of humour and fantasy.

pt-economy.title: pt-traditions.c9.text
Portugal's economy: Saudade is a longing for someone or something absent: a person, a place, a time, even something that may never return. It can feel sad and sweet at once.\n\nThe Portuguese often call it untranslatable and see it as part of the national character. It runs through fado, poetry and everyday speech: "tenho saudades tuas" means "I miss you".

pt-economy.title: pt-sport.c0.text
Portugal's economy: Football is Portugal's most popular sport. Three clubs, Benfica, FC Porto and Sporting, have won almost every league title since the league began in the 1930s.\n\nOnly two other clubs have ever been champions: Belenenses in 1946 and Boavista in 2001. Each of the big three has millions of supporters at home and abroad.

pt-economy.title: pt-sport.c1.text
Portugal's economy: Eusébio da Silva Ferreira, born in Mozambique in 1942, became one of the greatest strikers in history with Benfica and Portugal.\n\nNicknamed the Black Panther, he won the Ballon d'Or in 1965 and was top scorer at the 1966 World Cup, where Portugal finished third.

pt-economy.title: pt-sport.c2.text
Portugal's economy: Cristiano Ronaldo, born in Funchal, Madeira, in 1985, is one of the most successful footballers ever. He has won five Ballon d'Or awards and five Champions League titles.\n\nHe is the top scorer and most capped player in men's international football, and captained Portugal to its first trophies.

pt-economy.title: pt-sport.c3.text
Portugal's economy: For decades Portugal's national team played attractive football but won nothing. That changed at Euro 2016 in France, when Portugal beat the hosts 1–0 in the final.\n\nThey added the first UEFA Nations League in 2019, at home in Porto, and won it again in 2025, beating Spain on penalties in Munich.

pt-economy.title: pt-sport.c4.text
Portugal's economy: Roller hockey, or hóquei em patins, is played on four-wheeled roller skates with a stick and a hard ball. Portugal is one of the sport's great powers.\n\nIts men's team has won the world championship more than 15 times, rivalled mainly by Spain, Argentina and Italy.

pt-economy.title: pt-sport.c5.text
Portugal's economy: In winter, Praia do Norte in Nazaré produces some of the biggest surfable waves on Earth. An undersea canyon focuses the energy of Atlantic storms.\n\nSurfers towed in by jet-ski have ridden waves of over 25 metres there. Portugal's whole coast, from Peniche to Ericeira, is a surfing destination.

pt-economy.title: pt-sport.c6.text
Portugal's economy: Portugal's first Olympic gold medal came in the marathon: Carlos Lopes won in Los Angeles in 1984, aged 37.\n\nFour years later Rosa Mota won the women's marathon in Seoul, becoming Portugal's first female Olympic champion. Together they made distance running a national passion.

pt-economy.title: pt-sport.c7.text
Portugal's economy: After the marathon golds, Fernanda Ribeiro won the 10,000 m in Atlanta in 1996 with a fierce final lap.\n\nNelson Évora and Pedro Pichardo later won the triple jump, and in Paris 2024 Iúri Leitão and Rui Oliveira took gold in track cycling. Portugal has won six Olympic golds in all.

pt-economy.title: pt-sport.c8.text
Portugal's economy: The Volta a Portugal, first held in 1927, is the country's great cycling stage race. Each summer it crosses the country for about ten days, with crowds lining the mountain climbs.\n\nPortuguese riders have also shone abroad, from Joaquim Agostinho in the Tour de France to world champion Rui Costa and João Almeida.

pt-economy.title: pt-sport.c9.text
Portugal's economy: With a long Atlantic coast and a seafaring past, Portugal has a strong sailing tradition. Portuguese sailors won Olympic silver in 1948 and bronze in 1996.\n\nLisbon and Cascais regularly host major regattas, and the steady summer north wind makes the coast a favourite for windsurfing and kitesurfing.
